title: Chapter 12: Factor Markets, Labor Demand, and Wage Determination

questions.title: Roles of Households and Firms in Factor Markets
questions.prompt_template: In the Circular Flow model, what distinguishes factor markets from product markets?

hints.text: Compare who acts as the buyer and who acts as the seller in the top and bottom loops of the Circular Flow diagram.
In factor markets, businesses purchase the four productive inputs—labor, land, capital, and entrepreneurship—from households.

options_template.text: In factor markets, businesses demand productive inputs (labor, land, capital, and entrepreneurship) that are supplied by households.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Factor markets reverse the buyer-seller roles of product markets: households supply labor, land, capital, and entrepreneurship, while firms buy these inputs to produce output.

options_template.text: In factor markets, households demand finished consumer goods while businesses supply raw natural resources.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Circular Flow Reversal): Households demand finished goods in product markets, whereas in factor markets households are the suppliers of inputs and firms are the buyers.

options_template.text: Factor markets include only wage labor, while capital and land are traded exclusively inside product markets.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Incomplete Input Scope): Factor markets cover all four factors of production—labor, land, capital, and entrepreneurship—not just labor.

options_template.text: Factor markets are regulated government exchanges where output prices are fixed before production begins.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institutional Mischaracterization): Factor markets are decentralized markets where input prices such as wages and rents are determined by supply and demand, not government price-fixing bureaus.

questions.title: Meaning of Derived Demand for Labor
questions.prompt_template: Why do economists classify a firm's demand for labor as a 'derived demand'?

hints.text: Think about why a business hires software engineers, nurses, or baristas in the first place.
Labor demand does not exist independently of what happens in the firm's output market.

options_template.text: Because labor demand is derived from the legal minimum wage set by state and federal regulators.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Regulatory Origin Confusion): Minimum wage laws set a price floor on wages, but the underlying demand curve for labor originates from output demand and worker productivity.

options_template.text: Because firms hire workers solely to produce goods and services that consumers want to buy in the output market.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Firms do not hire labor for its own sake; their willingness to pay for workers is derived directly from consumer demand for the final goods and services those workers help produce.

options_template.text: Because individual workers derive utility directly from supplying hours of labor rather than from leisure.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Demand Side Confusion): Worker preferences between work and leisure govern labor supply, whereas derived demand explains the employer's demand for inputs.

options_template.text: Because labor demand is mathematically derived by subtracting fixed capital costs from total accounting profit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Accounting Formula Confusion): Labor demand is determined by the marginal revenue product of labor (MRP_L), not by subtracting fixed costs from accounting profit.

questions.topic: Marginal Product vs. Marginal Revenue Product
questions.title: Distinguishing Physical Productivity from Marginal Revenue Product
questions.prompt_template: Which statement accurately distinguishes Marginal Product of Labor (MP_L) from Marginal Revenue Product of Labor (MRP_L)?

hints.text: Pay attention to the units of measurement for each variable: physical units versus dollars.
Remember that a profit-maximizing firm must compare dollars of extra revenue against dollars of extra wage cost.

options_template.text: MP_L is measured in dollars per hour, whereas MRP_L is measured in physical units of output per worker.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unit Inversion): The units are reversed—MP_L measures physical output (e.g., bags of coffee or haircuts), whereas MRP_L converts that output into dollars of extra revenue.

options_template.text: MP_L includes both labor and capital costs, whereas MRP_L excludes the selling price of the product.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Revenue Conflation): Neither MP_L nor MRP_L is a cost measure; MP_L tracks physical output and MRP_L incorporates the product's price or marginal revenue.

options_template.text: MP_L measures the extra physical units of output from one more worker, whereas MRP_L measures the extra dollar revenue that output generates.
options_template.feedback: Correct. MP_L = delta Q / delta L is in physical units, while MRP_L translates that physical output into dollar revenue (MP_L x P in a competitive product market) so it can be compared directly to the dollar wage W.

options_template.text: MP_L applies only in the long run when all inputs vary, whereas MRP_L applies only in the short run when capital is fixed.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Time-Horizon Misclassification): Both MP_L and MRP_L are defined holding other inputs fixed in the short run and are linked directly at every hiring level.

questions.title: Marginal Revenue Product for a Firm with Product Market Power
questions.prompt_template: For a firm with monopoly power in its product market, why is Marginal Revenue Product of Labor equal to MP_L x MR rather than MP_L x P?

hints.text: Recall how a monopolist's marginal revenue relates to its product price when it expands output along a downward-sloping product demand curve.
When selling additional units produced by an extra worker, the monopolist must lower the price on all units sold.

options_template.text: Because a monopolist pays lower wages than a competitive firm, reducing its marginal revenue per worker.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Factor vs. Product Market Confusion): Product-market monopoly power alters the relationship between output price P and marginal revenue MR, independent of whether the labor market is competitive.

options_template.text: Because diminishing marginal returns do not occur for a monopolist, so MP_L stays constant as output rises.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Production Function Error): Diminishing marginal returns is a physical property of short-run production with fixed capital and applies regardless of product market structure.

options_template.text: Because a monopolist faces a horizontal product demand curve where MR always exceeds P.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand Curve Slope Reversal): A competitive firm faces a horizontal demand curve (MR = P), whereas a monopolist faces a downward-sloping demand curve where MR < P.

options_template.text: Because selling the extra output requires lowering the product price on all units, making MR strictly less than P.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Under output market power, extra output pushes down the market price, so each extra unit adds MR < P to total revenue; by the chain rule, MRP_L = MP_L x MR < MP_L x P.

questions.topic: Marginal Factor Cost in Competitive Labor Markets
questions.title: Why MFC_L Equals the Wage for a Wage-Taking Firm
questions.prompt_template: In a perfectly competitive labor market, why does a single firm's Marginal Factor Cost of Labor (MFC_L) equal the going market wage rate (W)?

hints.text: Consider whether one small firm's hiring decision can move the market-wide wage rate.
If the firm can hire as many workers as it wants at the same market wage W, what is the extra cost of one additional worker?

options_template.text: Because the firm is a wage taker and can hire additional workers at the constant market wage without raising pay for existing employees.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A competitive firm represents a tiny share of the labor market, so its labor supply curve is horizontal at W; each extra worker adds exactly W to total payroll cost (MFC_L = W).

options_template.text: Because competitive firms are legally permitted to pay each new hire a lower wage than existing workers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wage Discrimination Misconception): Competitive firms pay the single prevailing market wage W to all identical workers; they do not cut wages on marginal hires.

options_template.text: Because every worker in a competitive market has an identical Marginal Product of Labor (MP_L) regardless of firm size.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Productivity Confusion): MFC_L is determined by the wage cost of hiring labor, whereas MP_L reflects physical output and diminishes as more workers share fixed capital.

options_template.text: Because fixed capital costs decline by W whenever a competitive firm adds an additional unit of labor.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed Cost Misconception): Fixed capital costs do not change with short-run hiring; total labor cost rises by W for each extra worker hired.

questions.title: Profit-Maximizing Hiring Condition for Indivisible Workers
questions.prompt_template: A competitive wage-taking firm hiring indivisible workers should continue adding workers up to the last worker for whom:

hints.text: Apply the marginal principle: compare the extra dollar revenue from hiring one more worker against the extra dollar cost.
Hiring a worker raises profit whenever the extra revenue they bring in is at least as large as their wage.

options_template.text: MP_L is maximized and marginal cost of output is zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Maximum Productivity Confusion): Stopping where MP_L peaks leaves profitable workers unhired as long as subsequent workers still generate MRP_L >= W.

options_template.text: MRP_L >= W, stopping before any worker whose MRP_L falls strictly below W.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Every worker whose Marginal Revenue Product equals or exceeds the wage (MRP_L >= W) adds non-negative profit; hiring a worker with MRP_L < W strictly reduces profit.

options_template.text: Total output Q reaches its maximum, regardless of the market wage W.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Output Maximization Fallacy): Maximizing physical output ignores labor cost; workers who add positive output can still lose money if MRP_L < W.

options_template.text: Total revenue equals total wage cost, leaving zero firm surplus above wages.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Surplus Fallacy): Equating total revenue to total wage cost hires far past the profit-maximizing point and destroys the firm's net surplus earned on earlier workers.

questions.title: Opportunity Cost of an Hour of Leisure
questions.prompt_template: In the individual labor supply model, what is the economic opportunity cost of choosing one additional hour of leisure?

hints.text: Remember that opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative foregone.
When a worker chooses not to work an extra hour, what concrete earnings do they give up?

options_template.text: The explicit dollar price of entertainment goods purchased during that hour.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Explicit Cost Tunnel Vision): Explicit recreation spending is separate from the time opportunity cost of leisure, which exists even if you spend the hour resting at home.

options_template.text: The employer's fixed capital cost per hour of plant operation.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Firm-Worker Perspective Confusion): Fixed capital costs are borne by the employer, not by the individual worker choosing between paid work and leisure.

options_template.text: The hourly wage rate (W) foregone by not spending that hour in paid work.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Every hour allocated to leisure is an hour not spent earning the hourly wage W, making W the direct opportunity cost (price) of leisure.

options_template.text: Zero, because leisure is a non-market activity that carries no monetary price tag.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero Implicit Cost Fallacy): Even though leisure has no cash ticket price, time is scarce, so foregone hourly earnings W represent a real implicit opportunity cost.

questions.topic: Substitution and Income Effects in Labor Supply
questions.title: Competing Effects of a Higher Hourly Wage on Individual Hours
questions.prompt_template: Assuming leisure is a normal good, how do the substitution effect and the income effect respond when an individual worker receives a higher hourly wage?

hints.text: Trace the substitution effect through the higher opportunity cost of leisure, and the income effect through higher purchasing power.
If leisure is a normal good, wealthier individuals want to consume more of it—which means working fewer hours.

options_template.text: Both the substitution effect and the income effect motivate the worker to supply more hours of labor.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Normal Good Income Effect Error): While the substitution effect increases hours worked, the income effect leads a worker to buy more normal-good leisure and work fewer hours.

options_template.text: Both the substitution effect and the income effect motivate the worker to take more leisure and work fewer hours.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Substitution Direction Reversal): A higher wage raises the opportunity cost of leisure, so the substitution effect pushes the worker away from leisure and toward more work.

options_template.text: The substitution effect encourages more leisure (fewer work hours), while the income effect encourages more work hours.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Effect Label Swap): The two effects are reversed—substitution makes leisure costlier (more work), whereas higher income encourages consuming more normal-good leisure (less work).

options_template.text: The substitution effect encourages working more hours, while the income effect encourages taking more leisure and working fewer hours.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A higher wage makes leisure more expensive (substitution effect -> work more) while also making the worker wealthier so they demand more normal-good leisure (income effect -> work less).

questions.title: Compensating Wage Differentials vs. Human Capital Premiums
questions.prompt_template: Which example best illustrates a compensating wage differential rather than a human capital premium?

hints.text: Distinguish pay differences driven by formal education/training from pay differences driven by non-wage job hazards or unpleasantness.
A compensating differential offsets undesirable working conditions for otherwise comparable skill levels.

options_template.text: Higher hourly pay offered to hazardous-waste technicians compared to equally trained workers performing safe indoor lab tasks.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A compensating wage differential is the extra pay required to attract workers into jobs with greater physical risk, unpleasant environments, or undesirable schedules, holding skill constant.

options_template.text: Higher salaries earned by board-certified cardiologists compared to entry-level medical scribes due to a decade of medical training.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Human Capital Conflation): Higher pay resulting from years of schooling, residency, and specialized training is a human capital premium, not a compensating differential.

options_template.text: Higher pay earned by a single firm's sales staff after consumer demand for the company's product unexpectedly surges.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Short-Run Demand Shock Confusion): A temporary wage spike from surging output demand reflects a rightward shift in derived labor demand rather than compensating for job disamenities.

options_template.text: Lower wages paid by a dominant rural employer compared to competitive urban employers for identical warehouse work.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Monopsony Markdown Confusion): Depressed wages from single-employer market power represent a monopsony markdown, not a compensating wage differential.

questions.title: Why Market Labor Supply Slopes Upward Even If Individuals Bend Backward
questions.prompt_template: Even if a high-earning neurosurgeon cuts back her weekly hours when her pay rises from $400 to $500 per hour, why does the market labor supply curve for an occupation still slope upward?

hints.text: Distinguish the intensive margin (hours of existing workers) from the extensive margin (new people entering the occupation).
Think about how students, career switchers, and non-participants respond to higher wages in a field.

options_template.text: Because individual workers can never experience an income effect larger than their substitution effect.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Empirical Denial of Backward Bend): Individual supply can indeed bend backward at very high wages when the income effect dominates the substitution effect.

options_template.text: Because higher occupational wages attract new entrants from other jobs, motivate students to train in the field, and draw non-participants into the workforce.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Even if some incumbent high earners trim hours, higher wages expand the total number of workers entering the occupation, keeping the competitive market labor supply curve upward-sloping.

options_template.text: Because employers always shift the labor demand curve rightward whenever wages increase.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Demand Curve Confusion): Higher wages do not shift labor demand rightward; market supply slopes upward because of worker entry responses on the supply side.

options_template.text: Because government licensing boards automatically lower training requirements whenever wages rise.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institutional Assumption Error): Licensing standards do not automatically relax with wage increases; upward-sloping market supply comes from voluntary worker entry.

questions.title: Defining a Monopsony in Factor Markets
questions.prompt_template: What defines a monopsony in a labor market?

hints.text: Contrast a single seller in a product market (monopoly) with a single buyer in an input market (monopsony).
Think of a rural hospital system, remote mining company, or dominant regional distribution hub.

options_template.text: A labor market where a single labor union negotiates wages on behalf of all workers against many competing firms.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Buyer-Seller Side Reversal): A single organized seller of labor is a union (monopoly seller of labor), whereas a monopsony is a single or dominant buyer (employer) of labor.

options_template.text: A product market where one firm is the sole seller of a finished good with no close substitutes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Monopoly vs. Monopsony Confusion): A sole seller in a product market is a monopoly; a monopsony is a sole or dominant buyer in a factor market.

options_template.text: A labor market dominated by a single buyer (or dominant employer) that faces the entire upward-sloping local labor supply curve.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A monopsony exists when one dominant employer is the primary buyer of labor in a local market, giving it wage-setting power along the upward-sloping supply curve.

options_template.text: A competitive labor market where the government fixes the wage below the market-clearing equilibrium.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price Control Mischaracterization): Monopsony arises from employer market concentration on the demand side of labor, not from a government wage ceiling.

questions.title: Why Marginal Factor Cost Exceeds the Wage Under Monopsony
questions.prompt_template: Under a uniform-wage payroll, why does a monopsonist's Marginal Factor Cost of Labor (MFC_L) lie strictly above the labor supply curve (MFC_L > W)?

hints.text: Think about what happens to existing workers' wages when the monopsonist raises its wage offer to attract one additional worker.
Remember that under a uniform pay scale, the higher wage cannot be limited solely to the newly hired employee.

options_template.text: Because monopsonists are required by law to pay overtime premiums to all new workers from their first hour.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Statutory Overtime Confusion): MFC_L > W arises purely from facing an upward-sloping labor supply curve under a uniform wage, not from overtime statutes.

options_template.text: Because additional workers in a monopsony always have negative Marginal Product of Labor (MP_L < 0).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Productivity Confusion): MFC_L measures labor cost from the supply side, not worker productivity on the demand side.

options_template.text: Because the monopsonist must buy extra capital equipment that costs more than the worker's wage.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Capital Cost Conflation): Short-run MFC_L measures only the incremental labor payroll cost of hiring one more unit of labor, holding capital fixed.

options_template.text: Because attracting an additional worker requires offering a higher wage, which under a uniform pay scale must also be paid to all existing workers.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Total labor cost rises by the new worker's wage PLUS the wage increase granted to every previously hired worker, making MFC_L strictly greater than the wage W.

questions.title: Economic Source of Monopsony Deadweight Loss
questions.prompt_template: Why does a profit-maximizing monopsonist's hiring choice (L_M < L_C) generate deadweight loss for society?

hints.text: Compare the value of output produced (MRP_L) against the reservation wage (W) for workers between L_M and L_C.
Deadweight loss reflects mutually beneficial exchanges that fail to occur.

options_template.text: Because workers between L_M and L_C would generate more revenue (MRP_L) than the minimum wage they require to work (W), yet remain unhired.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Restricting employment to L_M leaves unrealized gains from trade: every unhired worker between L_M and L_C has MRP_L > W, so society forfeits the triangle of surplus between those curves.

options_template.text: Because the monopsonist hires too many workers past L_C, where wages exceed workers' Marginal Revenue Product.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Over-Hiring Direction Error): A monopsonist under-hires (L_M < L_C) to hold down wages; deadweight loss comes from too little employment, not excessive hiring.

options_template.text: Because every dollar of wage reduction paid to the L_M employed workers is destroyed rather than transferred to the firm.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Transfer vs. Deadweight Loss Confusion): Lower wages on the L_M employed workers represent a transfer of surplus from workers to the monopsonist, not deadweight loss.

options_template.text: Because a monopsonist always earns negative economic profits in the long run.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Profitability Error): Monopsony power typically increases employer profits at the expense of worker surplus and overall efficiency.

questions.title: Why a Competitive Firm's Labor Demand Curve Slopes Downward
questions.prompt_template: Holding the competitive product price (P) and short-run capital stock fixed, why does a firm's labor demand curve (D_L = MRP_L) slope downward?

hints.text: Look at the two components of MRP_L = MP_L x P and identify which one changes as L increases.
Think about what happens to extra output per worker when more employees share a fixed amount of floor space or machines.

options_template.text: Because a competitive firm must cut its output price P every time it hires another worker.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Competitive Price-Taker Violation): A firm selling in a competitive product market takes P as constant; the downward slope does not come from falling P.

options_template.text: Because diminishing marginal returns cause MP_L to decline as additional workers share a fixed capital stock, lowering MRP_L = MP_L x P.
options_template.feedback: Correct. With P fixed, diminishing marginal returns reduce MP_L as L increases, causing MRP_L to slope downward and trace out the firm's labor demand curve.

options_template.text: Because workers demand lower hourly wages when the firm employs a larger workforce.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Demand Curve Confusion): Worker wage preferences define labor supply, not the downward slope of a firm's MRP_L labor demand curve.

options_template.text: Because fixed capital costs rise proportionally with every new worker hired.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed Cost Misconception): Fixed capital costs do not vary with L in the short run and do not determine the slope of MRP_L.

questions.topic: Movements vs. Shifts of Labor Demand
questions.title: Wage Change vs. Output Price Change on a Firm's Labor Demand Graph
questions.prompt_template: On a competitive firm's labor demand diagram (wage on the vertical axis, labor on the horizontal axis), how does a decrease in the market wage (W) differ graphically from an increase in the product's selling price (P)?

hints.text: Check whether each variable is plotted on an axis of the labor market graph or held constant behind the curve.
Changes in the vertical-axis price (W) cause movements along a curve; changes in external determinants (P or MP_L) shift the curve.

options_template.text: A lower market wage shifts D_L rightward, whereas a higher product price causes a downward movement along D_L.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement-Shift Reversal): This swaps the two mechanisms—the wage W is on the vertical axis (movement along D_L), while product price P shifts MRP_L = MP_L x P.

options_template.text: Both a lower market wage and a higher product price shift the firm's D_L curve rightward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Axis-Variable Shift Error): A lower market wage shifts the horizontal S_L = MFC_L line downward and moves the firm down along its fixed D_L curve; it does not shift D_L.

options_template.text: A lower market wage causes a movement downward along the existing D_L curve (increasing L*), whereas a higher product price shifts the entire D_L = MRP_L curve rightward.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because W is measured on the vertical axis, a fall in W moves the firm down along its given MRP_L curve; because P multiplies MP_L at every L, a higher P shifts the entire MRP_L curve rightward.

options_template.text: Neither event changes optimal employment L*, because short-run physical productivity MP_L is unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Physical-Only Tunnel Vision): Hiring depends on comparing dollar MRP_L = MP_L x P to dollar W; both a lower W and a higher P raise optimal employment L*.

questions.title: Identifying Net Firm Surplus on the Competitive Labor Demand Graph
questions.prompt_template: In a competitive firm's labor demand diagram where a downward-sloping MRP_L curve intersects a horizontal wage line at (L*, W*), which geometric region represents the firm's net surplus above total wage payments?

hints.text: Recall that each worker contributes MRP_L in revenue and costs W* in wages, so the net gain on each worker is the vertical gap (MRP_L - W*).
Sum the vertical gaps (MRP_L - W*) from L = 0 up to L = L*.

options_template.text: The rectangle bounded below the horizontal wage line W* from L = 0 to L = L*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wage Bill Conflation): The rectangle W* x L* equals the firm's total wage bill paid to workers, not the firm's net surplus above wages.

options_template.text: The entire trapezoid under the MRP_L curve from L = 0 to L = L* down to the horizontal axis.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total Revenue Conflation): The full area under MRP_L from 0 to L* equals total revenue generated by labor, before subtracting total wage payments.

options_template.text: The triangle beneath the horizontal wage line W* and to the right of the MRP_L curve beyond L*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unprofitable Region Error): Beyond L*, W* > MRP_L, so hiring in that region would represent losses rather than positive firm surplus.

options_template.text: The triangle bounded above by the MRP_L curve and below by the horizontal wage line W* from L = 0 to L = L*.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Integrating the net marginal gain (MRP_L - W*) across all hired workers from 0 to L* forms the triangle between the MRP_L curve and the wage line W*.

questions.title: Graphical Effect of Productivity-Enhancing AI Tools on Software Engineers
questions.prompt_template: When generative AI coding assistants act as a capital complement that boosts software engineers' Marginal Product of Labor (MP_L), how does the competitive labor market diagram for software engineers adjust (ceteris paribus)?

hints.text: Determine how an increase in MP_L affects MRP_L = MP_L x P at every level of employment.
Trace the intersection of the new labor demand curve with the upward-sloping market labor supply curve.

options_template.text: Market labor demand (D_L) shifts rightward, raising both the equilibrium wage (W*) and equilibrium employment (L*).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Higher MP_L raises MRP_L at every employment level, shifting D_L rightward along an upward-sloping S_L curve and increasing both W* and L*.

options_template.text: Market labor demand (D_L) shifts leftward, lowering both the equilibrium wage (W*) and equilibrium employment (L*).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Substitute-Complement Confusion): A leftward shift of D_L occurs when capital substitutes for labor, not when complementary tools raise workers' MP_L.

options_template.text: Market labor supply (S_L) shifts rightward, lowering the equilibrium wage (W*) and raising employment (L*).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Supply Shift Swap): Capital tools that change worker productivity directly alter firms' MRP_L (labor demand), not households' labor supply curve.

options_template.text: Both D_L and S_L stay fixed, while firms move upward along D_L to a lower level of employment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Static Curve Fallacy): A change in MP_L directly changes the MRP_L schedule, shifting the entire labor demand curve rather than leaving it fixed.

questions.title: Graphical Effect of Automated Self-Checkout Kiosks on Routine Cashiers
questions.prompt_template: When grocery chains adopt automated self-checkout kiosks that directly substitute for routine manual checkout labor, how does the competitive labor market for routine cashiers adjust (ceteris paribus)?

hints.text: Ask whether automated kiosks raise or lower firms' demand for human cashiers at any given wage.
Shift the affected curve along an unchanged upward-sloping labor supply curve.

options_template.text: Labor supply (S_L) shifts leftward, raising the equilibrium wage (W*) and reducing employment (L*).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Side Misattribution): Adopting labor-saving checkout machines is a firm-side input substitution decision that shifts labor demand, not labor supply.

options_template.text: Labor demand (D_L) shifts leftward, lowering both the equilibrium wage (W*) and equilibrium employment (L*).
options_template.feedback: Correct. When lower-cost capital substitutes directly for routine tasks, firms demand fewer cashiers at every wage, shifting D_L leftward and pushing both W* and L* downward.

options_template.text: Labor demand (D_L) shifts rightward, raising the equilibrium wage (W*) while reducing employment (L*).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction and Equilibrium Inconsistency): Substitutes reduce rather than increase demand, and a rightward demand shift along upward-sloping supply raises both W* and L*.

options_template.text: Quantity of labor demanded falls along a fixed D_L curve because kiosk adoption automatically raises the statutory minimum wage.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Policy-Technology Conflation): Technological substitution shifts the D_L curve itself; it does not impose a minimum wage or cause a movement along a fixed demand curve.

questions.title: Effect of Stricter Occupational Licensing Requirements
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a state introduces longer mandatory training hours and tougher licensing exams to enter a skilled trade, holding derived labor demand constant. How does this shift the competitive labor market graph?

hints.text: Determine whether tougher licensing barriers change firms' willingness to pay (demand) or workers' cost of entering the occupation (supply).
Trace the new equilibrium along an unchanged downward-sloping labor demand curve.

options_template.text: Labor supply (S_L) shifts rightward, lowering the equilibrium wage (W*) and expanding employment (L*).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift Direction Reversal): Higher entry barriers reduce the number of qualified workers willing and able to supply labor at any wage, shifting S_L leftward rather than rightward.

options_template.text: Labor demand (D_L) shifts leftward, lowering both the equilibrium wage (W*) and equilibrium employment (L*).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Supply Misattribution): Licensing rules restrict worker entry on the supply side of the labor market rather than shifting consumers' derived demand for output.

options_template.text: Labor supply (S_L) shifts leftward, raising the equilibrium wage (W*) and reducing equilibrium employment (L*).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Tougher licensing restricts entry into the trade at every wage, shifting S_L leftward along D_L—which drives up the equilibrium wage W* and lowers equilibrium employment L*.

options_template.text: Labor demand (D_L) shifts rightward, raising both the equilibrium wage (W*) and equilibrium employment (L*).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Side Entry Confusion): Entry restrictions contract labor supply (raising W* while cutting L*); they do not shift D_L rightward.

questions.title: Impact of Higher Wages in an Alternative Occupation
questions.prompt_template: Electricians and HVAC technicians draw from a similar pool of technical-school graduates. If a construction boom sharply raises wages for electricians, how does the competitive labor market for HVAC technicians adjust (ceteris paribus)?

hints.text: Think about how a higher wage in a closely related career changes the opportunity cost of working as an HVAC technician.
Does this spillover shift HVAC labor demand or HVAC labor supply?

options_template.text: HVAC labor demand shifts rightward, raising both HVAC wages and HVAC employment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Side Spillover Error): Higher wages in an alternative occupation affect where workers choose to supply their labor, not firms' MRP_L for HVAC technicians.

options_template.text: HVAC labor supply shifts rightward, lowering HVAC wages and expanding HVAC employment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Migration Direction Error): Higher electrician wages pull workers out of HVAC into electrical work, reducing—not expanding—the supply of HVAC technicians.

options_template.text: HVAC labor demand shifts leftward, lowering both HVAC wages and HVAC employment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Curve Identification Error): Worker mobility across alternative jobs shifts the labor supply curve S_L, not the derived labor demand curve D_L.

options_template.text: HVAC labor supply shifts leftward, raising equilibrium HVAC wages (W*) and reducing equilibrium HVAC employment (L*).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Higher pay in an alternative occupation pulls workers away from HVAC jobs at every wage, shifting HVAC labor supply leftward, driving up W*, and lowering L*.

questions.title: Simultaneous Rightward Shifts in Labor Demand and Labor Supply
questions.prompt_template: Suppose booming consumer demand for cybersecurity services shifts derived labor demand for analysts rightward at the same time new university degree programs shift labor supply rightward. Without knowing the relative size of the two shifts, what can be predicted graphically?

hints.text: Draw both curves shifting right and compare the direction each shift pushes L* and W*.
When two shifts push a variable in opposite directions, its net change is ambiguous unless you know which shift is larger.

options_template.text: Equilibrium employment (L*) unambiguously increases, while the net change in the equilibrium wage (W*) is ambiguous.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Both rightward shifts expand employment (L* rises unambiguously), whereas higher demand pushes W* up and higher supply pushes W* down, leaving the net effect on W* ambiguous.

options_template.text: Equilibrium wage (W*) unambiguously increases, while the net change in equilibrium employment (L*) is ambiguous.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ambiguous Variable Swap): Both rightward shifts reinforce higher employment; it is the wage W*—not employment L*—that faces opposing upward and downward pressures.

options_template.text: Both equilibrium wage (W*) and equilibrium employment (L*) unambiguously increase.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Supply-Side Wage Pressure): Expanding labor supply puts downward pressure on wages; if the supply shift exceeds the demand shift, W* can actually fall.

options_template.text: Both equilibrium wage (W*) and equilibrium employment (L*) remain unchanged because the two shifts cancel each other out.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Complete Cancellation Fallacy): Simultaneous rightward shifts reinforce each other on quantity L*, guaranteeing strictly higher employment even if W* happens to stay near its starting value.

questions.topic: Short-Run vs. Long-Run Labor Supply Slope
questions.title: Comparing Steep Short-Run Supply to Flatter Long-Run Supply
questions.prompt_template: Following a large rightward shift in derived demand for registered nurses, how does the graphical adjustment along a steep (inelastic) short-run labor supply curve compare to the adjustment along a flatter (elastic) long-run labor supply curve?

hints.text: Visualize a rightward shift in D_L intersecting first a steep S_L curve and then a flatter S_L curve starting from the same initial equilibrium.
Steeper supply means quantity responds slowly while wages absorb more of the demand shock.

options_template.text: Short-run steep supply produces a smaller wage jump and a larger employment increase than long-run flat supply.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Elasticity-Slope Reversal): A steep (inelastic) supply curve restricts quantity expansion and forces a larger—not smaller—wage jump.

options_template.text: Short-run steep supply produces a larger wage spike and a smaller employment gain, whereas long-run flatter supply moderates the wage increase and yields a larger employment gain.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When supply is steep (inelastic) in the short run due to licensing and training lags, higher demand mostly bids up wages; as long-run supply flattens with new graduates, employment expands more and wage pressure moderates.

options_template.text: Both steep and flat supply curves produce the exact same equilibrium wage W*, differing only in employment L*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Wage Assumption): The slope of labor supply directly governs how a demand shift splits between wage changes and employment changes; flatter supply leads to a lower new wage than steeper supply.

options_template.text: Short-run steep supply causes employment to fall when demand increases, whereas long-run flat supply causes employment to rise.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Negative Slope Error): A steep upward-sloping supply curve still has a positive slope, so a rightward shift in D_L increases employment in both the short run and the long run.

questions.title: Geometric Relationship Between Linear S_L and MFC_L
questions.prompt_template: If a uniform-wage monopsonist faces a linear upward-sloping inverse labor supply curve W = a + bL (with a > 0 and b > 0), how is its Marginal Factor Cost curve (MFC_L) drawn on the graph?

hints.text: Recall Total Labor Cost TLC(L) = W(L) x L = aL + bL^2 and the resulting linear MFC_L equation from Section 12.3.
Compare both the vertical intercept (at L = 0) and the slope of MFC_L = a + 2bL against W = a + bL.

options_template.text: Parallel to the labor supply curve S_L, shifted upward by a constant vertical distance equal to a.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Parallel Shift Error): MFC_L is not parallel to S_L; because the wage increase applies to more existing workers as L grows, the vertical gap between MFC_L and S_L widens with L.

options_template.text: Starting at the origin (0, 0) with half the slope of the labor supply curve S_L.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intercept and Slope Inversion): MFC_L starts at the same positive vertical intercept a as S_L and has twice—not half—the slope.

options_template.text: Starting at the same vertical intercept a as S_L, with twice the slope (MFC_L = a + 2bL), lying strictly above S_L for all L > 0.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Just as a linear monopolist's MR has twice the slope of demand, a linear monopsonist's MFC_L = a + 2bL shares the vertical intercept a with S_L and rises twice as steeply.

options_template.text: Coinciding identically with the labor supply curve S_L up to L_M, and vertical thereafter.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Competitive Assumption Error): MFC_L coincides with S_L only for a wage-taking firm facing horizontal supply (or over the flat segment created by a minimum wage), not for an unconstrained monopsonist.

questions.topic: Reading Monopsony Equilibrium Off the Graph
questions.title: Locating the Monopsony Wage W_M on the Diagram
questions.prompt_template: On a standard monopsony diagram (showing MRP_L, S_L, and MFC_L), after finding optimal employment L_M where MRP_L intersects MFC_L, how do you read the monopsonist's wage W_M from the graph?

hints.text: Ask yourself which curve shows the minimum wage required to induce L_M workers to accept employment.
Do not confuse the marginal revenue product at L_M with the wage needed to attract L_M workers.

options_template.text: Read W_M directly from the vertical height of the intersection where MRP_L = MFC_L.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intersection Height Fallacy): The height where MRP_L = MFC_L equals the marginal worker's revenue product (and marginal factor cost), which is strictly higher than the wage needed to hire L_M workers.

options_template.text: Read W_M from the intersection of MRP_L and S_L.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Competitive Benchmark Error): Where MRP_L intersects S_L gives the competitive wage W_C and employment L_C, not the monopsony outcome.

options_template.text: Read W_M by moving horizontally from the vertical intercept of MRP_L.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intercept Confusion): The vertical intercept of MRP_L is the choke wage at L = 0, not the profit-maximizing monopsony wage.

options_template.text: Drop vertically from L_M down to the labor supply curve S_L and read W_M on the vertical axis.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Once L_M is set by MRP_L = MFC_L, the labor supply curve S_L tells the monopsonist the lowest uniform wage W_M sufficient to attract exactly L_M workers.

questions.topic: Minimum Wage Floor on a Monopsony Graph
questions.title: How a Minimum Wage Alters a Monopsonist's Effective MFC_L Curve
questions.prompt_template: Suppose the government imposes a minimum wage equal to the competitive wage (W_min = W_C) on a monopsonist. How does this change the shape of the monopsonist's effective Marginal Factor Cost curve?

hints.text: For any worker willing to work at or below W_C, does hiring an extra worker force the employer to raise wages for existing workers?
Check what happens to effective MFC_L both up to L_C and beyond L_C.

options_template.text: It becomes horizontal at W_C from L = 0 up to L_C, and then jumps vertically up to the original MFC_L curve for L > L_C.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because the firm must pay W_C anyway for all workers up to L_C, hiring additional workers up to L_C adds only W_C to payroll (flat MFC_L = W_C); beyond L_C, attracting more workers requires raising wages above W_C, so MFC_L jumps back to the original curve.

options_template.text: It shifts downward below the labor supply curve S_L for all levels of employment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Below-Supply Impossibility): A firm can never hire workers at a marginal factor cost strictly below the minimum wage workers require on S_L.

options_template.text: It remains completely unchanged, while the MRP_L curve shifts rightward to intersect MFC_L at L_C.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Shift Misattribution): A minimum wage floor alters the firm's marginal labor cost schedule (MFC_L), not workers' physical productivity or output price (MRP_L).

options_template.text: It becomes vertical at L_M, preventing the monopsonist from hiring any additional workers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Employment Fallacy): By eliminating the inframarginal wage-raise effect up to L_C, a wage floor at W_C flattens MFC_L and encourages the monopsonist to expand hiring from L_M to L_C.

questions.topic: Binding Minimum Wage in Competitive Labor Markets
questions.title: Graphical Effect of a Binding Minimum Wage Under Competition
questions.prompt_template: In a competitive labor market diagram, what occurs graphically when a binding minimum wage W_min is set strictly above the competitive equilibrium wage W_C?

hints.text: Draw a horizontal line at W_min > W_C and compare the horizontal coordinates where it meets D_L and S_L.
Remember that in a competitive market, actual employment is determined by the shorter side of the market.

options_template.text: Quantity of labor demanded exceeds quantity of labor supplied, creating a persistent labor shortage.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Floor vs. Ceiling Confusion): A labor shortage occurs when a binding price ceiling is set below W_C; a floor above W_C produces a labor surplus (unemployment).

options_template.text: Quantity of labor supplied exceeds quantity of labor demanded at W_min, creating a labor surplus (unemployment) while actual employment falls along D_L.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Above W_C, more workers want jobs (L_s > L_C) while competitive firms cut back hiring along D_L (L_d < L_C), creating a horizontal gap (L_s - L_d) of unemployment.

options_template.text: The entire labor demand curve D_L shifts rightward until the new equilibrium wage equals W_min.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Automatic Demand Shift Fallacy): A statutory wage floor does not shift D_L rightward; firms move upward and leftward along their existing D_L curve.

options_template.text: Both wages and employment rise simultaneously to the point where W_min intersects the labor supply curve S_L.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Monopsony-Competition Conflation): Simultaneous increases in wages and employment can happen under monopsony, but in a competitive market firms refuse to hire workers whose MRP_L < W_min.

questions.title: Profit-Maximizing Hiring and Net Surplus for an Artisan Bakery
questions.prompt_template: An artisan bakery sells sourdough loaves in a competitive product market for P = $12 per loaf and hires bakers in a competitive labor market at W = $150 per day. With fixed ovens in the short run, daily output is Q(0) = 0, Q(1) = 18, Q(2) = 34, Q(3) = 48, Q(4) = 58, and Q(5) = 64 loaves. How many bakers should the bakery hire, and what is its net daily surplus above total wages?

hints.text: First compute MP_L = delta Q for each baker, then multiply each MP_L by P = $12 to find MRP_L.
Hire every baker whose MRP_L >= $150, then sum (MRP_L - $150) across those hired bakers—or compute (Total Revenue - Total Wage Cost).

options_template.text: Hire 4 bakers; net daily surplus above wages is $96.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Marginal Loss on 4th Worker): The 4th baker adds MP_L = 10 loaves, generating MRP_L = $120 < $150, which cuts daily profit by $30 (from $126 down to $96).

options_template.text: Hire 3 bakers; net daily surplus above wages is $576.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total Revenue vs. Net Surplus): $576 is total daily revenue (48 loaves x $12); subtracting total wages (3 x $150 = $450) leaves a net surplus of $126.

options_template.text: Hire 3 bakers; net daily surplus above wages is $126.
Hire 5 bakers; net daily surplus above wages is $18.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Output Maximization Fallacy): Hiring the 4th and 5th bakers increases physical output but loses $30 and $78 respectively because both have MRP_L < $150.

questions.title: Linear Labor Demand Equilibrium and Firm Surplus Area
questions.prompt_template: A competitive wage-taking firm has a linear Marginal Revenue Product of Labor schedule MRP_L = 80 - 5L (in dollars per hour) and faces a competitive market wage of W* = $30 per hour. What are the firm's profit-maximizing employment (L*) and hourly firm surplus above wages?

hints.text: Set MRP_L = W* to solve for optimal employment L*.
Firm surplus is the triangle area 1/2 x base x height, where base = L* and height = (vertical intercept of MRP_L - W*).

options_template.text: L* = 10 workers; firm surplus = $500 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Missing Triangle Factor): Computing base x height = 10 x ($80 - $30) = $500 gives a rectangle rather than a triangle; multiplying by 1/2 yields $250.

options_template.text: L* = 16 workers; firm surplus = $250 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Wage Intercept Error): Setting 80 - 5L = 0 finds the horizontal intercept L = 16 instead of equating MRP_L to W* = $30.

options_template.text: L* = 10 workers; firm surplus = $300 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wage Bill Substitution): $300 = $30 x 10 is the firm's hourly total wage bill, whereas firm surplus above wages is the triangle area 1/2 x 10 x ($80 - $30) = $250.

options_template.text: L* = 10 workers; firm surplus = $250 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting 80 - 5L = 30 gives 5L = 50, so L* = 10 workers. Hourly firm surplus is 1/2 x 10 x ($80 - $30) = $250 per hour.

questions.topic: Output Price Impact on Derived Labor Demand
questions.title: Hiring Response to a Product Price Increase
questions.prompt_template: A competitive berry farm has physical Marginal Product of Labor MP_L = 24 - 2L crates per hour and hires pickers in a competitive labor market at W = $24 per hour. Initially, berries sell for P_1 = $3 per crate. If booming demand raises the market price to P_2 = $6 per crate (holding W fixed at $24), by how many workers does the farm's optimal hiring increase?

hints.text: Construct MRP_L = P x MP_L at P_1 = $3 and solve MRP_L = $24 for L_1*.
Repeat at P_2 = $6 to find L_2*, then take the difference (L_2* - L_1*).

options_template.text: Optimal hiring increases by 2 workers (from 8 to 10 workers).
options_template.feedback: Correct. At P_1 = $3, 3(24 - 2L) = 24 gives 24 - 2L = 8 -> L_1* = 8. At P_2 = $6, 6(24 - 2L) = 24 gives 24 - 2L = 4 -> L_2* = 10. Hiring rises by 10 - 8 = 2 workers.

options_template.text: Optimal hiring increases by 8 workers (from 8 to 16 workers).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Proportional Scaling Fallacy): Doubling the output price doubles MRP_L at each L, but because of the constant intercept and diminishing MP_L, optimal L* does not double.

options_template.text: Optimal hiring increases by 4 workers (from 8 to 12 workers).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope Division Error): The required MP_L drops by 4 crates (from 8 to 4), but because MP_L falls by 2 crates per worker, dividing 4 by 2 yields an increase of 2 workers, not 4.

options_template.text: Optimal hiring remains unchanged at 8 workers because MP_L did not change.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MP_L vs. MRP_L Confusion): Even with unchanged physical MP_L, a higher output price P raises MRP_L = MP_L x P and expands profit-maximizing employment.

questions.title: Computing MRP_L for a Firm with Output Market Power
questions.prompt_template: A local monopolist currently employs 4 workers who produce 40 units per hour, sold at a price of P = $20 per unit. Hiring a 5th worker raises output by MP_L = 10 units (to 50 units per hour), but to sell all 50 units the firm must lower its price to P = $18 per unit on every unit sold. What is the 5th worker's Marginal Revenue Product of Labor (MRP_L)?

hints.text: Remember that MRP_L is the change in total revenue (delta TR) caused by hiring the 5th worker.
Compute TR(40) = 40 x $20 and TR(50) = 50 x $18, then find TR(50) - TR(40).

options_template.text: $180 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Competitive Formula Misapplication): Multiplying MP_L x P_2 = 10 x $18 = $180 ignores the $2 price reduction lost on the 40 inframarginal units (40 x $2 = $80).

options_template.text: $100 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Total revenue rises from TR(40) = 40 x $20 = $800 to TR(50) = 50 x $18 = $900, so MRP_L = $900 - $800 = $100 per hour (equivalently, MR = $100 / 10 = $10, and MP_L x MR = 10 x $10 = $100).

options_template.text: $200 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Old-Price Valuation Error): Multiplying MP_L x P_1 = 10 x $20 = $200 assumes the firm can sell the extra 10 units without lowering price at all.

options_template.text: $10 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MR vs. MRP_L Confusion): $10 is the marginal revenue per unit of output (MR = $100 / 10 units), not the total extra revenue generated by the 5th worker (MP_L x MR = $100).

questions.title: Solving Linear Competitive Labor Demand and Supply
questions.prompt_template: In a competitive regional market for dental hygienists, labor demand is L_d = 900 - 12W and labor supply is L_s = 180 + 8W, where W is the hourly wage in dollars and L is the number of hygienists employed. What are the equilibrium hourly wage (W*) and equilibrium employment (L*)?

hints.text: Set quantity of labor demanded equal to quantity of labor supplied: L_d = L_s.
Collect all W terms on one side and constant terms on the other, solve for W*, and substitute W* back into both equations to verify L*.

options_template.text: W* = $54 per hour; L* = 612 hygienists.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intercept Addition Sign Error): Adding 900 + 180 = 1,080 instead of subtracting 900 - 180 = 720 produces W = 1,080 / 20 = $54, where L_d = 252 does not equal L_s = 612.

options_template.text: W* = $36 per hour; L* = 288 hygienists.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Supply Intercept): Evaluating 8 x 36 = 288 forgets to add the +180 intercept in L_s = 180 + 8W.

options_template.text: W* = $36 per hour; L* = 468 hygienists.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting 900 - 12W = 180 + 8W yields 720 = 20W, so W* = $36/hr. Substituting into L_s gives 180 + 8(36) = 468 hygienists (check: 900 - 12(36) = 468).

options_template.text: W* = $180 per hour; L* = 1,620 hygienists.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope Subtraction Sign Error): Subtracting 12W - 8W = 4W instead of adding 12W + 8W = 20W gives an invalid wage of 720 / 4 = $180/hr.

questions.topic: Comparative Statics of Labor Demand Shifts
questions.title: Wage and Employment Changes After a Rightward Demand Shift
questions.prompt_template: In a competitive market for solar installers, initial labor demand is L_d1 = 1,000 - 20W and labor supply is L_s = 100 + 10W. Suppose new clean-energy incentives increase labor demand by 300 installers at every wage, so L_d2 = 1,300 - 20W (holding supply constant). By how much do the equilibrium wage (delta W*) and equilibrium employment (delta L*) change?

hints.text: Solve for the initial equilibrium (W_1*, L_1*) using L_d1 = L_s, then solve for the new equilibrium (W_2*, L_2*) using L_d2 = L_s.
Alternatively, use the linear comparative-statics multipliers: delta W* = delta alpha / (d + b) and delta L* = [d / (d + b)] x delta alpha.

options_template.text: delta W* = +$10 per hour; delta L* = +300 installers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Horizontal Shift Conflation): The demand curve shifts right by 300 workers at a fixed wage, but rising wages along upward-sloping supply temper hiring so employment rises by only 100.

options_template.text: delta W* = +$30 per hour; delta L* = +300 installers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Demand Slope): Dividing the 300-worker shift solely by the supply slope (10) ignores the demand slope (20) in the denominator (b + d = 30).

options_template.text: delta W* = +$15 per hour; delta L* = +150 installers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Supply Slope): Dividing 300 solely by the demand slope (20) omits the supply slope (10); the correct denominator is 20 + 10 = 30.

options_template.text: delta W* = +$10 per hour; delta L* = +100 installers.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Initial equilibrium is 1,000 - 20W = 100 + 10W -> W_1* = $30, L_1* = 400. New equilibrium is 1,300 - 20W = 100 + 10W -> W_2* = $40, L_2* = 500. Thus delta W* = +$10/hr and delta L* = +100 installers.

questions.title: Calculating Point Wage Elasticity of Labor Supply
questions.prompt_template: In a competitive market for biomedical technicians, market labor supply is L_s = 150 + 5W, and the market clears at equilibrium W* = $30 per hour and L* = 300 technicians. What is the point wage elasticity of labor supply (epsilon_{L,s}) at this equilibrium, and how is supply classified?

hints.text: Use the point elasticity formula from Section 12.2: epsilon_{L,s} = (dL_s / dW) x (W* / L*).
Identify the slope dL_s / dW = 5, multiply by W* / L* = 30 / 300, and check whether the result is less than or greater than 1.

options_template.text: epsilon_{L,s} = 0.50 (inelastic labor supply).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Using epsilon_{L,s} = (dL_s / dW) x (W* / L*) = 5 x (30 / 300) = 150 / 300 = 0.50. Because 0.50 < 1, labor supply is wage-inelastic at this equilibrium.

options_template.text: epsilon_{L,s} = 2.00 (elastic labor supply).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Elasticity Ratio): Computing L* / (5 x W*) = 300 / 150 = 2.00 inverts the elasticity formula, reversing numerator and denominator.

options_template.text: epsilon_{L,s} = 5.00 (elastic labor supply).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Elasticity Equivocation): The number 5 is the linear slope dL_s / dW, not the dimensionless elasticity; you must multiply by W* / L* = 30 / 300.

options_template.text: epsilon_{L,s} = 0.10 (inelastic labor supply).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Slope Term): Computing only W* / L* = 30 / 300 = 0.10 omits multiplying by the supply slope dL_s / dW = 5.

questions.title: Computing Marginal Factor Cost Under a Uniform Wage Scale
questions.prompt_template: A remote mining company currently employs 8 haul-truck drivers at $25 per hour. To attract a 9th driver under a uniform pay scale, the firm must raise the hourly wage to $27 per hour for all drivers. What is the Marginal Factor Cost (MFC_L) of hiring the 9th driver?

hints.text: Calculate Total Labor Cost (TLC = L x W) at 8 drivers and again at 9 drivers.
Subtract TLC(8) from TLC(9)—or add the 9th driver's $27 wage to the $2 raise paid to each of the 8 existing drivers.

options_template.text: $27 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wage-Taking Assumption Error): $27 is only the 9th driver's wage; under a uniform pay scale, you must also include the $2/hr raise given to the 8 existing drivers ($16).

options_template.text: $43 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Correct. TLC(8) = 8 x $25 = $200 and TLC(9) = 9 x $27 = $243, so MFC_L = $243 - $200 = $43 per hour (equivalently, $27 + 8 x $2 = $43).

options_template.text: $45 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double-Counting the Marginal Worker's Raise): Adding 9 x $2 = $18 to $27 double-counts the $2 raise on the 9th driver, whose full wage is already included in $27.

options_template.text: $16 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted New-Hire Wage): $16 (= 8 x $2) measures only the inframarginal raise paid to existing drivers, omitting the $27/hr wage paid to the 9th driver.

questions.title: Solving for Monopsony Hiring and Wage from Linear Curves
questions.prompt_template: A regional hospital monopsonist faces an inverse labor supply curve W = 20 + 2L (with Marginal Factor Cost MFC_L = 20 + 4L) and Marginal Revenue Product MRP_L = 80 - 2L, where W is the hourly wage in dollars and L is measured in tens of nurses (so L = 1 represents 10 nurses). What are the monopsonist's profit-maximizing employment and hourly wage?

hints.text: Equate MRP_L = MFC_L to solve for L_M (remembering to multiply by 10 to convert to individual nurses).
Substitute L_M into the inverse labor supply curve W = 20 + 2L—not into MFC_L or MRP_L—to find W_M.

options_template.text: 100 nurses at W_M = $60 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reading Wage Off MRP_L / MFC_L): $60 is MRP_L(10) = MFC_L(10); the monopsonist pays the lower wage needed on the labor supply curve S_L, W_M = 20 + 2(10) = $40.

options_template.text: 150 nurses at W_M = $50 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Competitive Equilibrium Substitution): Setting MRP_L = W solves for the competitive benchmark (L_C = 15, W_C = $50) rather than the monopsony optimum (MRP_L = MFC_L).

options_template.text: 100 nurses at W_M = $40 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting MRP_L = MFC_L gives 80 - 2L_M = 20 + 4L_M -> 60 = 6L_M -> L_M = 10 (100 nurses). Reading off labor supply gives W_M = 20 + 2(10) = $40 per hour.

options_template.text: 150 nurses at W_M = $80 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double Rule Violation): Solving for competitive employment L_C = 15 and plugging it into MFC_L = 20 + 4(15) = $80 violates both the hiring rule and the wage-setting curve.

questions.title: Computing Hourly Deadweight Loss Under Monopsony
questions.prompt_template: A rural lumber mill is a monopsonist facing inverse labor supply W = 10 + 0.5L, Marginal Factor Cost MFC_L = 10 + L, and Marginal Revenue Product MRP_L = 70 - 0.5L, where L is the number of workers and W is the hourly wage in dollars. What is the hourly deadweight loss (DWL) created by monopsony power?

hints.text: First find the monopsony outcome (L_M, W_M, and MRP_L at L_M) using MRP_L = MFC_L, and the competitive benchmark L_C using MRP_L = W.
Compute the DWL triangle area: 1/2 x (L_C - L_M) x [MRP_L(L_M) - W_M].

options_template.text: $400 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted 1/2 Triangle Factor): Multiplying (L_C - L_M) x (MRP_L(L_M) - W_M) = 20 x $20 = $400 gives a rectangle rather than the DWL triangle area of $200.

options_template.text: $100 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Half-Height Wedge Error): Using only W_C - W_M = $40 - $30 = $10 as the triangle height omits the upper half of the DWL wedge between MRP_L(40) = $50 and W_C = $40.

options_template.text: $600 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Triangle Base): Using total competitive employment L_C = 60 as the base instead of the employment shortfall (L_C - L_M = 20) overstates DWL by a factor of three.

options_template.text: $200 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Monopsony sets 70 - 0.5L = 10 + L -> L_M = 40, with W_M = $30 and MRP_L(40) = $50. Competition sets 70 - 0.5L = 10 + 0.5L -> L_C = 60. Thus DWL = 1/2 x (60 - 40) x ($50 - $30) = 1/2 x 20 x $20 = $200 per hour.

questions.title: Employment Effect of an Intermediate Minimum Wage Under Monopsony
questions.prompt_template: A dominant regional employer faces inverse labor supply W = 14 + L, Marginal Factor Cost MFC_L = 14 + 2L, and Marginal Revenue Product MRP_L = 62 - L (where L is the number of workers and W is the hourly wage). Without regulation, it hires L_M = 16 workers at W_M = $30/hr (below competitive L_C = 24, W_C = $38/hr). If the state imposes a minimum wage of W_min = $35 per hour, how many workers will the firm hire?

hints.text: At W_min = $35/hr, find how many workers are willing to supply labor on S_L: W = 14 + L.
Check whether MRP_L at that supply quantity still exceeds $35/hr, and whether the original MFC_L jumps above MRP_L for any additional worker.

options_template.text: 21 workers (employment expands by 5 workers above L_M = 16).
options_template.feedback: Correct. At W_min = $35, labor supply is L_s = 35 - 14 = 21 workers, where effective MFC_L is flat at $35 and MRP_L(21) = 62 - 21 = $41 > $35. Hiring a 22nd worker would require raising wages above $35, pushing MFC_L to 14 + 2(22) = $58 > $40, so the firm hires exactly 21 workers.

options_template.text: 27 workers (determined by setting MRP_L = $35).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring the Labor Supply Constraint): Although MRP_L(27) = $35, only L_s = 35 - 14 = 21 workers are willing to work at $35/hr; hiring beyond 21 forces wages above $35 and raises MFC_L sharply above MRP_L.

options_template.text: 16 workers (employment remains unchanged at L_M).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Static Monopsony Quantity Error): Because the $35 wage floor eliminates the inframarginal raise penalty up to 21 workers, workers 17 through 21 all have MRP_L > $35 and are now profitable to hire.

options_template.text: 11 workers (employment falls by 5 workers below L_M = 16).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Competitive Minimum Wage Misapplication): Assuming a wage floor always cuts employment ignores that W_min = $35 lies between W_M = $30 and W_C = $38, flattening MFC_L and expanding monopsony hiring.

questions.title: Using Labor Supply Elasticity to Compute Monopsony MRP_L
questions.prompt_template: Using the monopsony optimization condition MRP_L = W x (1 + 1 / epsilon_{L,s}), suppose a dominant employer pays a uniform wage of W = $25 per hour in a local labor market where the wage elasticity of labor supply is epsilon_{L,s} = 2.5. What is the worker's Marginal Revenue Product (MRP_L) at the monopsony optimum?

hints.text: First compute the reciprocal of the labor supply elasticity: 1 / 2.5.
Add 1 to (1 / 2.5), then multiply the result by the monopsony wage W = $25.

options_template.text: $62.50 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direct Elasticity Multiplication): Multiplying W x epsilon_{L,s} = $25 x 2.5 = $62.50 ignores both the reciprocal (1 / epsilon_{L,s}) and the base wage term (1 + ...).

options_template.text: $35.00 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Since 1 / 2.5 = 0.40, MRP_L = $25 x (1 + 0.40) = $25 x 1.40 = $35.00 per hour—reflecting a 40% markdown wedge relative to the $25 wage.

options_template.text: $87.50 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Uninverted Elasticity Error): Computing $25 x (1 + 2.5) = $87.50 forgets to invert epsilon_{L,s}; more elastic labor supply must shrink the markdown, not enlarge it.

options_template.text: $10.00 per hour.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Markdown Gap Only): $25 / 2.5 = $10.00 equals only the dollar wedge (MRP_L - W), omitting the $25 wage itself.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Generative AI Raises Demand for Some Workers While Lowering It for Others
questions.prompt_template: Using the derived-demand framework (MRP_L = MP_L x P), why does adopting new digital and AI technologies tend to push up wages for senior engineers while reducing hiring for workers performing routine, automatable clerical tasks?

hints.text: Distinguish whether new capital serves as a complement to a worker's skills or a direct substitute for the worker's core tasks.
Connect each relationship to the direction of the shift in D_L = MRP_L.

options_template.text: Because technology always lowers the output price P to zero for clerical firms while raising P for software firms.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Only Misattribution): Even holding output prices constant, technology shifts labor demand differently depending on whether capital complements or substitutes for human tasks.

options_template.text: Because routine clerical workers have backward-bending market labor supply curves, whereas senior engineers have horizontal supply curves.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Side Misattribution): The diverging wage and employment effects stem from opposite shifts in labor demand (complements vs. substitutes), not backward-bending market supply.

options_template.text: Because AI acts as a capital complement that boosts MP_L (shifting D_L right) for complex engineering roles, while acting as a capital substitute that replaces tasks (shifting D_L left) for routine clerical roles.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Technological change is not uniform across occupations: complementary tools raise MP_L and shift D_L rightward, whereas task-automating substitutes shift D_L leftward.

options_template.text: Because minimum wage laws prevent firms from paying engineers less, whereas clerical workers are exempt from wage floors.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Minimum Wage Misattribution): Wage divergence between high-skill engineers and routine tasks occurs well above statutory wage floors due to derived-demand shifts.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: How Output-Market Monopoly Power Reduces Labor Hiring
questions.prompt_template: Consider two firms that share the exact same production function MP_L and hire labor in the exact same competitive labor market at wage W. Firm A sells output in a competitive product market, while Firm B is a monopolist in its product market. Why does Firm B hire fewer workers than Firm A?

hints.text: Compare Firm A's MRP_L = MP_L x P against Firm B's MRP_L = MP_L x MR.
Because a monopolist restricts output to keep price high, how does that affect its derived demand for labor?

options_template.text: Because Firm B faces an upward-sloping Marginal Factor Cost curve (MFC_L > W) even in a competitive labor market.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Monopsony-Monopoly Conflation): Both firms hire in a competitive labor market (MFC_L = W); Firm B's market power is in the product market, not the labor market.

options_template.text: Because Firm B's workers experience faster diminishing marginal returns than Firm A's workers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Production Function Assumption Violation): The problem specifies that both firms share the exact same physical MP_L schedule.

options_template.text: Because Firm B is required to pay compensating wage differentials to attract workers into a monopolized industry.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Compensating Differential Misattribution): Product-market monopoly power does not inherently make jobs more hazardous or require compensating differentials.

options_template.text: Because Firm B's marginal revenue is strictly below price (MR < P), making its labor demand curve (MP_L x MR) lie below Firm A's (MP_L x P) at every employment level.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because a product-market monopolist must cut price to sell extra output (MR < P), each worker adds less marginal revenue than under competition, causing Firm B to restrict both output and labor hiring.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Diagnosing the 'Hire Until MP_L = 0' Management Fallacy
questions.prompt_template: A factory supervisor proposes hiring additional assembly workers as long as each new worker adds positive physical output (MP_L > 0), arguing that 'more output always means more profit.' Why is this hiring strategy flawed when the market wage W is positive?

hints.text: Compare the extra revenue brought in by a worker whose MP_L is very small (but positive) against the wage W the firm must pay.
Check the marginal profit condition: delta profit = MRP_L - W.

options_template.text: Because once MRP_L falls below the positive wage W, hiring another worker with 0 < MRP_L < W adds less to revenue than to payroll cost, strictly reducing profit.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Positive physical output does not guarantee positive marginal profit; profit-maximizing firms stop at MRP_L = W rather than continuing until MP_L = 0.

options_template.text: Because hiring any worker in the region of diminishing marginal returns (MP_L falling) automatically causes total output to decline.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Diminishing vs. Negative Returns Confusion): Diminishing marginal returns means MP_L is falling while still positive (so total output still rises); the flaw is ignoring that MRP_L has dropped below W.

options_template.text: Because wages W automatically become zero whenever MP_L reaches zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wage-Adjustment Fallacy): A competitive firm takes the market wage W as fixed regardless of its own workers' MP_L.

options_template.text: Because total revenue is maximized only when MP_L is at its highest peak, before diminishing returns begin.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Peak MP_L vs. Maximum Revenue Error): Total revenue keeps rising as long as MRP_L > 0, and profit peaks where MRP_L = W—both well past the peak of MP_L.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Short-Run Wage Spikes vs. Long-Run Supply Expansion in Nursing
questions.prompt_template: As an aging population expands derived demand for registered nurses, hospitals often experience sharp short-run spikes in travel-nurse pay and sign-on bonuses. Based on Chapter 12's factor-market analysis, which policy best addresses long-run nursing shortages without creating permanent price-control distortions?

hints.text: Recall why short-run nursing supply is steep (inelastic): multi-year coursework, clinical rotations, and state board exams.
Compare policies that flatten and shift long-run labor supply against policies that cap wages or restrict supply.

options_template.text: Imposing a permanent wage ceiling below the market-clearing wage so hospitals can afford to hire more nurses.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wage Ceiling Shortage Fallacy): Capping wages below equilibrium reduces quantity of nurses supplied while raising quantity demanded, worsening rather than solving the nursing shortage.

options_template.text: Expanding nursing school faculty, clinical-rotation slots, and training capacity to make long-run labor supply flatter and shift it rightward.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Relaxing training bottlenecks allows higher wages to translate into larger nursing-school enrollments and graduations, flattening and shifting long-run S_L rightward to expand employment and moderate wage pressure.

options_template.text: Raising state licensing fees and lengthening residency requirements to ensure fewer new nurses enter the market.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Restriction Backfire): Tougher entry barriers shift S_L leftward, driving wages even higher while reducing the number of practicing nurses.

options_template.text: Subsidizing hospital demand for inpatient procedures while keeping nursing school capacity fixed.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Only Amplification): Boosting healthcare demand further against an inelastic short-run supply curve only pushes wages higher without expanding nursing capacity.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Interpreting Persistent Pay Gaps Between Equally Skilled Workers
questions.prompt_template: Two maintenance technicians possess identical certifications and years of experience, yet one earns $12 per hour more working overnight winter shifts on remote offshore wind turbines than the other earns working daytime shifts in a mild urban office park. How does factor-market equilibrium explain why this wage gap persists without everyone moving to offshore turbines?

hints.text: Evaluate both the monetary wage and the non-monetary working conditions (safety risk, isolation, schedule) of each job.
In equilibrium, workers weigh total job compensation—pay plus amenities/disamenities.

options_template.text: Because offshore wind companies are legally prohibited from hiring urban technicians.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Artificial Barrier Assumption): The gap persists even with free worker mobility because many workers prefer safer, daytime urban jobs despite the lower wage.

options_template.text: Because urban office technicians must have strictly higher human capital than offshore turbine technicians.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Premise Contradiction): The scenario holds certifications and experience equal, and higher human capital would raise—not lower—urban pay.

options_template.text: Because the $12/hr premium is a compensating wage differential needed to attract enough labor supply into a riskier, less convenient work environment.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Fewer workers are willing to supply labor to harsh, overnight offshore jobs at any given wage (a leftward-positioned supply curve), so equilibrium requires a persistent compensating differential to equalize total job attractiveness.

options_template.text: Because offshore wind operators must be monopsonists, and monopsonists always pay higher wages than competitive urban firms.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Monopsony Wage Direction Error): Monopsony power depresses wages below competitive levels (W_M < W_C); it does not explain a persistent wage premium.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Reconciling Reduced Incumbent Hours with Higher Total Market Employment
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a broad reduction in marginal income tax rates raises after-tax hourly wages for specialized surgeons.
