Empirically, a few senior partners cut back from 55 to 48 hours per week, yet total surgical employment across the region increases. How does Chapter 12 reconcile these two simultaneous observations?

hints.text: Separate the response of a high-earning individual already in the field from the aggregate market supply response across potential entrants.
Link the senior partners' cutback to the income vs. substitution effect and market expansion to new entry.

options_template.text: The data must be contradictory because individual and market labor supply curves always slope in the exact same direction at every wage.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fallacy of Composition): Individual supply can bend backward at very high wages even while market supply slopes upward due to entry from other specialties and delayed retirements.

options_template.text: The tax cut shifted labor demand leftward for senior partners while shifting labor demand rightward for junior surgeons.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Side Misattribution): Personal income tax rate changes alter workers' after-tax take-home wage on the supply side, not hospitals' MRP_L.

options_template.text: Senior partners cut hours because leisure became an inferior good after the tax cut.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inferior Good Direction Error): If leisure were an inferior good, higher after-tax income would reduce leisure and increase—not decrease—hours worked.

options_template.text: For high-earning senior partners, the income effect outweighed the substitution effect (backward-bending individual supply), while higher after-tax pay attracted new entrants and delayed retirements (upward-sloping market supply).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Individual high earners can buy more normal-good leisure when after-tax wages jump, while higher after-tax earnings still expand total market labor supply along the extensive margin.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Theoretical Reconciliation of Card and Krueger (1994)
questions.prompt_template: In their landmark 1994 study of fast-food restaurants along the New Jersey-Pennsylvania border, David Card and Alan Krueger observed that New Jersey's minimum wage increase was not accompanied by the sharp job losses predicted by a basic competitive labor market model. Which theoretical mechanism from Chapter 12 helps explain how a moderate minimum wage increase can avoid job losses—or even raise employment?

hints.text: Think about how employer wage-setting power alters the effect of a moderate wage floor.
Recall what happens to a monopsonist's effective Marginal Factor Cost when a wage floor is set near W_C.

options_template.text: Local monopsony power arising from commuting costs, scheduling constraints, and job-search frictions allows a moderate wage floor to flatten employers' MFC_L and raise wages and employment simultaneously.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When frictions give employers upward-sloping labor supply curves (local monopsony power), a moderate minimum wage set between W_M and W_C eliminates the marginal hiring penalty on existing payroll, supporting higher pay without job losses.

options_template.text: Fast-food restaurants face horizontal labor supply curves, so raising the minimum wage shifts their labor demand curve rightward automatically.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Competitive Shift Fallacy): Under horizontal competitive labor supply, a binding minimum wage above W_C causes firms to move up along D_L and cut hiring rather than shifting D_L rightward.

options_template.text: Higher minimum wages reduce worker productivity MP_L, which forces restaurants to hire more workers to produce the same number of meals.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Productivity-Loss Hiring Fallacy): Lower MP_L reduces MRP_L and shifts labor demand leftward, reducing rather than increasing profit-maximizing hiring.

options_template.text: Minimum wages eliminate diminishing marginal returns in restaurant kitchens, making MRP_L upward-sloping.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Production Function Alteration Error): A statutory wage floor changes labor cost, not the physical law of diminishing marginal returns.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Policy Limits of Minimum Wages Under Monopsony
questions.title: Identifying When a Minimum Wage Cuts Employment Even Under Monopsony
questions.prompt_template: A policy analyst argues that because a local labor market exhibits monopsony power, raising the minimum wage to ANY higher level will always increase employment. What exact boundary from Chapter 12's monopsony model refutes this claim?

hints.text: Check the height of the monopsonist's MRP_L curve at the initial monopsony employment level L_M.
What happens if W_min is set higher than MRP_L(L_M)?

options_template.text: Any minimum wage above W_M immediately cuts employment below L_M because monopsonists never expand hiring when wages rise.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Competitive Reflex Error): Over the range W_M < W_min <= MRP_L(L_M), flattening MFC_L raises monopsony employment above L_M (peaking at W_min = W_C).

options_template.text: Once a minimum wage is pushed above MRP_L(L_M), the marginal cost of hiring exceeds the marginal revenue product at L_M, forcing even a monopsonist to cut employment below L_M.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Monopsony reverses the competitive prediction only over a bounded range: pushing W_min above W_C reduces employment relative to L_C, and pushing W_min strictly above MRP_L(L_M) reduces employment below the original monopsony level L_M.

options_template.text: A minimum wage cuts monopsony employment only if it is set below the initial monopsony wage W_M.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Non-Binding Floor Confusion): A minimum wage set below W_M is non-binding and has no effect on wages or employment.

options_template.text: A minimum wage cuts monopsony employment only when labor supply is perfectly inelastic (vertical).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Elasticity Boundary Confusion): Regardless of supply elasticity, any wage floor pushed above workers' Marginal Revenue Product makes hiring unprofitable and cuts jobs.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Monopsony Power Persists Without a Literal Single-Company Town
questions.prompt_template: Modern empirical labor economists document meaningful local monopsony power in sectors like regional hospitals, retail chains, and suburban warehouses even when multiple firms operate within the same state. What real-world frictions create upward-sloping labor supply curves for individual employers?

hints.text: Ask why a worker cannot costlessly quit one employer and start at another employer 40 miles away the next morning.
Recall the concrete frictions highlighted in Section 12.3's Bring It Home case.

options_template.text: Zero commuting costs, instant job matching, and identical schedules across all employers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Perfect Competition Conditions): Frictionless mobility, zero search costs, and identical job traits describe a perfectly competitive labor market where each firm faces horizontal supply, not monopsony.

options_template.text: Perfectly elastic labor supply curves caused by nationwide uniform licensing reciprocity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Elasticity Direction Reversal): Perfectly elastic labor supply eliminates monopsony power (1 / infinity = 0 markdown); monopsony arises from inelastic/upward-sloping firm-level supply.

options_template.text: Commuting costs, family scheduling constraints, specialized skills, and job-search frictions that limit workers' ability to switch employers effortlessly.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When switching employers is costly due to commute distance, shift compatibility, specialized training, or search time, each firm faces an upward-sloping labor supply curve and exercises local monopsony power.

options_template.text: Competitive product markets that force every employer to set MRP_L equal to zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Product-Market Misattribution): Competitive product markets give MRP_L = MP_L x P > 0 and do not create employer monopsony power in labor markets.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: How Remote-Work Access Alters Local Monopsony Wage Markdowns
questions.prompt_template: Using the monopsony wage markdown relationship (MRP_L - W) / W = 1 / epsilon_{L,s}, how should the widespread adoption of high-speed internet and remote-work jobs affect the wage markdown exercised by a dominant rural employer?

hints.text: Determine whether access to remote national employers makes a rural employer's local labor supply more elastic or less elastic.
Plug a larger epsilon_{L,s} into the markdown ratio 1 / epsilon_{L,s}.

options_template.text: It lowers epsilon_{L,s}, allowing the rural employer to widen its wage markdown and pay even less relative to MRP_L.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Elasticity Direction Reversal): Better outside job options make local workers more responsive to wage differences—raising, not lowering, epsilon_{L,s}.

options_template.text: It leaves epsilon_{L,s} unchanged because remote employers cannot affect the wage elasticity of local workers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Closed-Market Assumption): Remote-work opportunities expand workers' relevant geographic labor market beyond commuting distance, directly increasing local supply elasticity.

options_template.text: It raises epsilon_{L,s}, which increases the ratio 1 / epsilon_{L,s} and widens the gap between MRP_L and W.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverse Relationship Error): Because epsilon_{L,s} is in the denominator of 1 / epsilon_{L,s}, a larger elasticity shrinks the markdown rather than widening it.

options_template.text: It raises epsilon_{L,s} by expanding workers' outside job options, shrinking the markdown 1 / epsilon_{L,s} and pushing local wages closer to MRP_L.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Greater outside employment alternatives make a local employer's labor supply more elastic (higher epsilon_{L,s}), eroding monopsony power and compressing the wage markdown toward competitive levels.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Uniform Minimum Wage Across Heterogeneous Markets
questions.title: Contrasting Effects of a Statewide Minimum Wage on Competitive vs. Monopsony Towns
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a state sets a single binding minimum wage moderately above current wages across both (1) a dense, highly competitive urban barista market and (2) an isolated rural town dominated by a single large food-processing plant. What contrasting outcomes does Chapter 12's factor-market theory predict?

hints.text: Apply the competitive labor market model to the urban barista market and the monopsony model to the isolated rural plant.
Check the employment impact in each market separately.

options_template.text: In the competitive urban market, employment is predicted to decline (creating a labor surplus), whereas in the monopsonistic rural town, a moderate wage floor between W_M and MRP_L(L_M) can raise both wages and employment.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Policy impacts depend critically on market structure: a binding floor above W_C reduces hiring along D_L under competition, while a moderate floor in a monopsony town flattens MFC_L and can expand both pay and jobs.

options_template.text: Employment is predicted to rise in the competitive urban market and fall in the monopsonistic rural town.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Market-Structure Reversal): This inverts the two theoretical predictions—competition yields a labor surplus above W_C, while monopsony permits simultaneous wage and employment gains.

options_template.text: Both markets will experience identical percentage reductions in employment because labor demand slopes downward in both.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Monopsony Omission): While D_L slopes downward in both markets, the monopsonist's hiring is initially constrained by MFC_L > W, so a moderate wage floor changes its marginal hiring calculus differently.

options_template.text: Neither market will experience any change in wages or employment because firms will simply pass 100% of wage costs onto consumers with zero change in quantity demanded.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Elasticity Product Demand Fallacy): Passing costs into higher prices reduces quantity of output demanded along downward-sloping product demand, which does not insulate competitive hiring from a binding wage floor.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Uniform Wage vs. Perfect Wage Discrimination
questions.title: Efficiency and Distribution Under Perfect Monopsony Wage Discrimination
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a monopsonist could legally pay each newly hired worker their exact reservation wage along S_L (perfect wage discrimination) rather than paying a single uniform wage to all employees. How would this change the monopsonist's Marginal Factor Cost, employment level, and deadweight loss?

hints.text: Ask whether hiring an additional worker still requires raising the wage paid to existing workers if the firm can pay individualized wages.
Compare the resulting hiring rule against the competitive efficiency benchmark MRP_L = W.

options_template.text: MFC_L would rise even steeper above S_L, cutting employment further below L_M and doubling deadweight loss.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Uniform-Raise Persistence Error): MFC_L lies above S_L solely because of the uniform-wage constraint; removing that constraint eliminates the inframarginal raise penalty.

options_template.text: MFC_L would collapse onto the labor supply curve S_L, expanding hiring to the competitive level L_C and eliminating deadweight loss—while transferring all worker surplus to the employer.
options_template.feedback: Correct. If each worker is paid only their own reservation wage on S_L, hiring one more worker costs just W(L) (MFC_L = S_L). The firm hires up to MRP_L = W at L_C, eliminating DWL while capturing the entire worker surplus.

options_template.text: Employment would stay stuck at L_M, but every worker would earn the competitive wage W_C.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wage and Quantity Misprediction): A perfectly wage-discriminating monopsonist pays lower-reservation workers less than W_C and expands hiring all the way to L_C.

options_template.text: Deadweight loss would disappear because every worker would receive a uniform wage equal to their MRP_L.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Distributional Mischaracterization): Efficiency (zero DWL) is achieved at L_C, but workers are paid their minimum reservation wages along S_L—not a uniform wage equal to MRP_L.
